sections.section_title: Clinical Presentation and Initial Diagnostic Dilemma
sections.description: The identification of monogenic diabetes often begins with recognizing a discrepancy between a patient's clinical phenotype and their expected physiological response to standard diabetic classifications. In this case, the index patient, a young adult male, presented not through acute emergency services but incidentally during an annual health examination. He exhibited marked hyperglycemia and glycosuria yet lacked the classic precipitating factors for either typical type 1 diabetes (autoimmune destruction) or type 2 diabetes (metabolic syndrome-driven insulin resistance). His Body Mass Index (BMI) was recorded at 24.6 kg/m², placing him within the normal range, and notably, he displayed no cutaneous stigmata of insulin resistance such as acanthosis nigricans. sections.section_title: Pathophysiological Mechanisms and Differential Diagnosis Strategy
sections.description: Understanding the unique pathophysiology of *HNF1A*-maturity-onset diabetes of the young (MODY) is essential for distinguishing it from the more prevalent forms of diabetes mellitus. Unlike Type 1 diabetes, characterized by autoimmune-mediated destruction of pancreatic $\beta$-cells, or Type 2 diabetes, driven primarily by peripheral insulin resistance and relative $\beta$-cell failure, *HNF1A*-MODY arises from a monogenic defect in a specific transcription factor. The *HNF1A* gene encodes hepatocyte nuclear factor 1-alpha, a protein critical for regulating the expression of numerous genes involved in glucose homeostasis across multiple tissues, including the liver, kidney, and pancreas. sections.section_title: Confirmatory Genetic Testing and Variant Interpretation
sections.description: Following the exclusion of autoimmune type 1 diabetes through negative serology and the recognition of a strong multigenerational family history suggestive of monogenic inheritance, the diagnostic pathway shifted toward molecular genetics. While clinical scoring systems, such as the Exeter MODY probability calculator, provided an initial estimate of likelihood, they cannot definitively distinguish between specific genetic etiologies or rule out phenocopies like early-onset type 2 diabetes. Consequently, next-generation sequencing (NGS) panels emerged as the gold standard for confirmation in this case.
